introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education (GCE) Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 2 (0560), Paper 2 - Modern World History Since 1870, ORDINARY LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: two and a half hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR Questions. TWO questions must be chosen from SECTION A, ONE from SECTION B and ONE other from SECTION C. One of the two questions chosen from SECTION A must be a Starred question.

Maps should be used to illustrate answers where appropriate. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION A: CAMEROON SINCE 1850**

Question one is compulsory. Answer either 1A\* or 1B\* and one other Question from this section.

**1. Either**

**A\* (Starred question)** *Study this extract bearing on German occupation and administration of Cameroon (1884-1916) and answer question a-e which follow. The maximum marks for each sub question is indicated in the brackets.*

*(The extract is set line by line as printed; the line numbers printed in the right margin are shown in square brackets. The questions refer to lines 1, 3, 4, 5 and 9.)*

> The intense scramble for Cameroon in the 1880's by some European powers ended with the signing of an annexation  
> treaty in July 1884.  
> The German official who championed this achievement for his country was... Then followed the appointment of an  
> interim commissioner pending the establishment of a permanent German colonial government in the territory.  
> In 1885, a pioneer Governor for Cameroon was appointed, who expanded German influence into the interior while [5]  
> German missionaries also implanted themselves in the territory.  
> Native reactions to German colonisation of their land was mixed, while, some favoured the Germans, others  
> vehemently rejected them.  
> In 1895 a ruthless and brutal Governor was appointed for the territory. During his rule, several innovations were  
> undertaken. [10]  
> Examples included the development of plantations and the establishment of German trading concessions ; that  
> traded with the Bamileke and Bamum and the other that traded with the Ewondo and Bulu people.  
> In 1906, a Douala chief petitioned this Governor to the German government in Berlin for his administrative excesses.  
> These complaints were investigated and some were found to be true .  
> This Governor was recalled, tried and found guilty. He was dismissed and sentenced to prison. [15]  
> The natives found favour in the new Governor who replaced the sentenced one.  
> Some scholars consider German rule to have been a mixed blessing to the natives whose endurance with the  
> Germans abruptly ended in 1916. [18]

**Source:** *Adopted from Germans in the Cameroons by Harry Rudin 1938.*

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a)

(i) Identify one European power that hotly contested the Scramble for Cameroon mentioned in **line 1**.

(ii) Write down the name of the German official mentioned in **line 3** who championed the annexation.

(iii) Identify the Interim Commissioner mentioned in **line 4** before the arrival of the German Governor.

(iv) Who was the pioneer German Governor for Cameroon mentioned in **line 5**?

**(1+1+1+1 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) A European power in the Scramble (1 mark).** **Britain**. Line 1 speaks of "some European powers": Britain, Germany and, to a lesser degree, France were the powers interested in the coast of Cameroon in the early 1880s. Britain was the power that hotly contested the German move: the Douala chiefs had asked Queen Victoria for protection since 1879, a British consul (Edward Hewett) was sent too late, and the British government condemned the German annexation. (Germany or France is also acceptable as a power that took part in the scramble.)

**(ii) The German official (1 mark).** **Dr Gustav Nachtigal**, the German explorer appointed Imperial Commissioner by Chancellor Bismarck. He signed a treaty in Togo on 5 July 1884, arrived at Douala on 11 July 1884, and had the German flag hoisted over Douala on 14 July 1884. (Bismarck gave the authority and the Hamburg merchant Adolph Woermann lobbied for the annexation, but Nachtigal was the official who carried it out on the spot.)

**(iii) The interim commissioner (1 mark).** **Max Buchner**, the German explorer who acted as interim Imperial Commissioner after Nachtigal left the coast in 1884, until a permanent colonial government was set up under a Governor.

**(iv) The pioneer Governor (1 mark).** **Julius von Soden** (Baron von Soden), the first German Governor of Cameroon (1885-1891). He chose Douala as the seat of the government, began to open trade routes into the interior and started the system of stations.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b)

(i) Give two reasons for the expansion of German influence into the interior.

(ii) Name an ethnic group that reacted positively to the German penetration and occupation and state the reason.

(iii) Identify an ethnic group that reacted negatively to the German occupation and state the reason.

**(2+2+2 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Two reasons for expansion into the interior (2 marks, 1 mark each).** Any two of the following:
- **Trade and raw materials.** The Germans wanted to reach the sources of palm products, rubber and ivory in the interior and to open new markets for German goods.
- **To break the Douala monopoly.** The Douala were middlemen who controlled the trade between the coast and the interior; the Germans wanted to trade directly with the inland peoples.
- **To make the claim effective.** After the Berlin Conference (1884-1885) a European power had to occupy the territory it claimed, so the Germans had to show their authority inland and prevent Britain and France from taking the hinterland.
- **Missionary and civilising aims.** German missionaries (Basel Mission, Pallottines) were also moving inland, as the extract says, and the government supported them.
- **Land for plantations and a source of labour and taxes** to make the colony pay for itself.

**(ii) A group that reacted positively (2 marks).** The **Bali (Bali-Nyonga)**, led by Fon Galega I, welcomed the Germans. **Reason:** the alliance gave them guns and military support, which they used against their neighbours (for example the Bafut and other Grassfields chiefdoms), and gave them trade, protection and, later, the Basel Mission schools. (The **Douala chiefs Bell and Akwa** also signed the 1884 treaty, hoping for protection of their trade; the **Bamum** under King Njoya later cooperated with the Germans too; any of these with a correct reason is accepted.)

**(iii) A group that reacted negatively (2 marks).** The **Bakweri** (around Buea and Mount Cameroon) fought the Germans. **Reason:** they were defending their land and independence; German stations, plantations, forced labour and the taking of their land threatened their way of life. Their chief **Kuva Likenye** won a famous victory at Buea in 1891, when the German expedition under Baron von Gravenreuth was beaten and its leader killed, before the Germans finally subdued them in the mid-1890s. (Other acceptable answers: the **Bafut**, the **Bulu** and **Beti**, **Lock Priso** of Hickory Town, **Bonabéri**, with the reason: loss of independence, taxation, forced labour, loss of trade or land.)
themes: indigenous resistance to german rule in cameroon

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c)

(i) Identify the ruthless and brutal German Governor mentioned in **line 9**.

(ii) Apart from plantations and trade State any other two positive developments carried out by the Governor mentioned in c (i).

**(1+2 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The Governor (1 mark).** **Jesko von Puttkamer**, Governor of Cameroon from 1895 until he was recalled in 1906-1907. He ruled during the great expansion of the plantations and the concession companies, and he was known for the harsh treatment of Africans (forced labour and flogging).

**(ii) Two positive developments other than plantations and trade (2 marks, 1 mark each).** Any two of:
- **Communications:** the building of roads and, from about 1906, of the first railways (the Northern Line from Douala towards Nkongsamba, and the start of the Central Line from Douala towards the interior), with port works at Douala, and the telegraph.
- **Administration:** the extension of the administrative stations and districts inland and the setting up of an organised colonial government; the seat of government was moved to the healthier **Buea** about 1901.
- **Education and health:** support to the missions that opened schools and hospitals, and the first government schools and health services.
- **Urban growth:** the growth of Douala and the building of the first modern buildings.

(The concession companies of 1899 and the plantations are the developments the question excludes.)

**(1+1+1+1 marks)**

questions.enonce_markdown:
(e)

(i) State the event that led to the abrupt end of German rule.

(ii) What legacy did the Germans leave in Cameroon before their abrupt departure?

**(1+2 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The event (1 mark).** The **outbreak of the First World War in August 1914**: British, French and Belgian forces invaded the German colony, took Douala (27 September 1914) and Yaoundé (1 January 1916) and forced the last German troops to flee into Spanish Rio Muni and to surrender at Mora (February 1916). The Treaty of Versailles (1919) then took the colony away from Germany for good.

**(ii) The German legacy (2 marks, 1 mark each).** Any two of:
- **Economic:** plantations (cocoa, bananas, rubber, oil palm), the first railways and roads, the port of Douala and the trading companies; the cash-crop economy.
- **Administrative and territorial:** the colony of Kamerun with its frontiers, which later became the basis of the two mandates, and the stations that became towns (Yaoundé, Buea, Douala).
- **Social:** Western education and Christianity through the Basel Mission, Baptist and Catholic missions, and the first African teachers, clerks and workers.
- **Negative:** forced labour, loss of land and the bitter memory of harsh rule (and, in the Douala case, the hanging of Rudolf Douala Manga Bell in August 1914).
